sessions.title: The WHS primary duty of care and the training duty
sessions.summary: Learn who owes the WHS primary duty, what 'reasonably practicable' means, the seven limbs of section 19(3) including the duty to provide information, training, instruction and supervision, and the due diligence officers must show.
objectives: Identify the PCBU, workers and others protected by the WHS Act
Apply the eliminate-then-minimise approach and the reasonably practicable test
Explain what section 19(3)(f) requires for information, training, instruction and supervision
Describe the officer's due diligence duty and the duties of workers

cards.title: Stage one: the safety brief that never happened
cards.setting: People Risk and Safety floor, Tasman Ridge Bank head office, Barangaroo, Sydney. 8:40 am.

lines.text: Your first morning as a workplace conduct and safety analyst at Tasman Ridge Bank. A printed incident summary is already waiting on your desk.
Welcome! I'm Leila Nasser, head of people risk and safety. That summary is from our Parramatta contact centre, and it is why you are here.

Ben Tran, team leader in Parramatta and our elected health and safety representative. Last week a new starter took six abusive calls in a row and left the floor in tears. Nobody had shown her how to end an abusive call.
Aroha Ngata, whistleblower protection officer. Safety, harassment and speaking up all land on our floor sooner or later, so you will see a lot of me too.
James Whitfield, chief operating officer. I am a registered accountable person and an officer for WHS purposes. When something goes wrong in operations, I need to know what the law expected of us.
Chloe Papadopoulos, branch manager in Hobart. My team handles cash, irate customers and late finishes. Training is not a nice-to-have for us.
Five stages, one final exam. First stage: the primary duty of care in the Work Health and Safety Act, and the training promise hidden inside it. Ready?

cards.title: Who owes the duty, and to whom

scenes.heading: The PCBU
scenes.narration: The WHS Act puts its main duty on a person conducting a business or undertaking, the PCBU. For us, the PCBU is the bank itself, whether or not an activity makes a profit.

scenes.heading: Workers, widely defined
scenes.narration: A worker is anyone who carries out work in any capacity for the PCBU: employees, contractors and their staff, labour hire workers, apprentices, students on placement and volunteers.

scenes.heading: The primary duty
scenes.narration: Section 19 requires the PCBU to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of its workers, and that other people, such as customers, are not put at risk by its work.

scenes.heading: Health means mind too
scenes.narration: The Act defines health as both physical and psychological health. A contact centre's emotional load counts just as much as a slippery floor.

scenes.heading: Officers and workers
scenes.narration: Officers must exercise due diligence so the bank complies, and every worker must take reasonable care and follow reasonable safety instructions. Everyone has a part.

cards.title: How 'reasonably practicable' is worked out
cards.caption: Section 18 lists the matters weighed. Section 17 adds the order: eliminate a risk if reasonably practicable; if not, minimise it.

items.label: Likelihood
items.detail: How likely is the hazard or risk to occur?

items.label: Degree of harm
items.detail: How serious could the harm be if it happens?

items.label: Knowledge
items.detail: What the bank knows, or ought reasonably to know, about the risk and ways to deal with it

items.label: Available controls
items.detail: Whether ways to eliminate or minimise the risk exist and suit the situation

items.label: Cost last
items.detail: Only after the steps above, the cost of controls, including whether it is grossly disproportionate to the risk

cards.question: A contractor's employee installs new teller screens in a Tasman Ridge branch. Is she a 'worker' to whom the bank owes the primary duty?
options: No, only the bank's own employees are workers
Yes, the definition of worker includes an employee of a contractor
Only if she has worked at the branch for more than three months
Only if her employer has no WHS policy of its own
cards.explanation: Section 7 defines a worker as anyone carrying out work in any capacity for a PCBU, expressly including employees of contractors and subcontractors. Neither length of engagement nor the contractor's own policy changes that.

cards.title: Section 19(3): the seven things the primary duty includes
cards.body:
Section 19(3) spells out what the primary duty includes, so far as is reasonably practicable:

- **(a)** a work environment without risks to health and safety
- **(b)** safe plant and structures
- **(c)** safe systems of work
- **(d)** safe use, handling and storage of plant, structures and substances
- **(e)** adequate welfare facilities, and access to them
- **(f)** any **information, training, instruction or supervision** needed to protect all persons from work-related risks
- **(g)** monitoring workers' health and workplace conditions to prevent illness or injury

Paragraph (f) is why the bank's WHS training is not optional. It is not limited to a single induction: the test is what is **necessary** to protect people from the risks of the work actually done. New tasks, new systems and new hazards mean new training, instruction or supervision.

cards.title: Who carries this duty?
cards.prompt: Sort each duty to the person the WHS Act places it on.

items.text: Ensure safe systems of work for cash handling
Provide training needed to protect people from work risks
Keep up-to-date knowledge of WHS matters
Verify that safety resources and processes are provided and used
Take reasonable care for their own health and safety
Follow reasonable safety instructions given by the bank
Monitor workplace conditions to prevent illness or injury
Understand the hazards of the bank's operations generally

cards.title: The turn: 'we sent them the policy'

lines.text: Here's the induction checklist. Item 14: 'Read the abusive caller policy.' It's ticked. But nobody practised a call, and nobody sat with her.
So the policy existed, the tick existed, and she still had no idea she was allowed to end the call.
Same in Hobart. We email the hold-up procedure once a year. I doubt half the team could tell you the first three steps.
Is emailing a document enough to say we provided training and instruction?
That's exactly the question. Section 19(3)(f) asks what is necessary to protect people. A document nobody understands may not be it.

cards.title: Fixing the contact centre induction
cards.situation: Tasman Ridge is about to on-board 30 new contact centre staff in Parramatta. Ben's review shows that abusive calls are frequent, the policy lets staff end a call after a warning, but new starters only read the policy and are placed on live calls on day two without a buddy. You must recommend a fix to Leila.

choices.text: Add practised call-handling sessions on abusive callers, a buddy on live calls for the first weeks, a clear rule that staff may end abusive calls, and check-ins with Ben as HSR
choices.outcome: This tackles the risk with training, instruction and supervision matched to the actual hazard, and consults the HSR. It is the kind of response s 19(3)(f) and s 49 point to.

choices.text: Re-send the policy with a request that new starters confirm they have read it
choices.outcome: A read-receipt proves delivery, not understanding or capability. The risk on live calls is largely unchanged.

choices.text: Keep the induction but offer a counselling service for anyone who is upset afterwards
choices.outcome: Support after harm matters, but it does not eliminate or minimise the risk first. Controls should come before the injury.

choices.text: Ask experienced staff to take all difficult calls so new starters are protected
choices.outcome: This shifts the hazard to another group without managing it, and may overload experienced staff. The underlying risk is still uncontrolled.

cards.title: PCBU duty versus officer due diligence
cards.caption: An officer can be found guilty of failing the s 27 duty whether or not the bank itself is convicted.

items.label: Who
items.left: The bank as a business or undertaking
items.right: Directors and senior people who make or influence decisions about the business

items.label: What
items.left: Ensure health and safety so far as reasonably practicable
items.right: Exercise due diligence so the bank complies with its duties

items.label: Knowledge
items.left: Know the risks of the work
items.right: Keep up-to-date WHS knowledge and understand the operations

items.label: Resources
items.right: Ensure resources and processes exist and are used

items.label: Evidence
items.left: Records of controls, training and consultation
items.right: Verify, not just assume, that it is all happening

cards.title: Officer due diligence in practice
cards.prompt: Match each element of due diligence in s 27(5) to what James might do as COO.

pairs.right: Attend a briefing on new psychosocial risk guidance each year
Spend a shift in the Parramatta contact centre and a Hobart branch
Approve budget for call-handling training and extra team leaders
Receive a monthly safety dashboard and act on trends quickly
Make sure HSR training requests and notifiable incidents are handled
Ask internal audit to test whether training actually took place

cards.question: Which statement about the officer's duty under s 27 is correct?
options: It only applies after the bank has been convicted of a WHS offence
It is met if the board has approved a WHS policy
It requires reasonable steps, including verifying that safety resources and processes are provided and used
It applies only to officers with a safety qualification
cards.explanation: Section 27(5) lists due diligence steps, ending with verifying the provision and use of resources and processes. Section 27(4) says an officer can be convicted whether or not the PCBU is, and approving a policy alone is not verification.

cards.title: Inside the story: Hobart's after-hours cash run
cards.body:
Chloe's Hobart branch closes at 4 pm but the vault is balanced and cash is prepared for collection after closing. A new teller, Sam, is rostered to help on his third day.

**What went wrong:** Sam had read the security procedure, but nobody had walked him through it. He propped the rear door open to carry out rubbish while cash was on the counter.

**What Chloe changed:**
- a short, practical walk-through of the closing procedure for every new team member before they join a close
- a buddy for the first two weeks of closes
- a laminated three-step card at the rear door
- a quick quarterly refresher, recorded in the learning system

Nothing happened to Sam, but the near miss showed a gap in **instruction and supervision** for a known risk. That is s 19(3)(f) in a bank branch: training is matched to the risk of the actual task, and supervision covers the gap until the person is competent.

cards.title: Which WHS law applies to your workplace?
cards.body: This quest uses the section numbers of the **Commonwealth Work Health and Safety Act 2011**, which follows the national model law. Most private-sector workplaces are covered by their **state or territory** WHS Act, built on the same model, so the duties look very similar. **Victoria** has its own Occupational Health and Safety Act with different numbering. Always check which law, regulator and codes apply where you work.

cards.title: Stage one take-aways
items: The bank, as a PCBU, must ensure workers' health and safety, and that of others, so far as is reasonably practicable
Health includes psychological health; workers include contractors, labour hire staff, students and volunteers
Section 19(3)(f) requires the information, training, instruction or supervision necessary to protect people from work risks
Eliminate risks first; if that is not reasonably practicable, minimise them, weighing cost last
Officers must exercise due diligence, including verifying that resources and processes are used; workers must take reasonable care

cards.prompt: Think of one task in your team that a new starter does in their first month. What information, training, instruction or supervision do they actually receive before doing it, and would it protect them if something went wrong?

quiz.question: Under the WHS Act, who owes the primary duty of care in section 19?
options: Each worker personally, for their own tasks and team
The state or territory WHS regulator for the area, acting on behalf of the Crown
The person conducting a business or undertaking (PCBU)
The elected health and safety representative
quiz.explanation: Section 19 places the primary duty on the PCBU. Workers have their own duties under s 28, and HSRs and regulators have functions, not the primary duty.

quiz.question: Which paragraph of section 19(3) deals with information, training, instruction and supervision?
options: Paragraph (f)
Paragraph (a), read with paragraph (e)
Paragraph (c)
Paragraph (g)
quiz.explanation: Section 19(3)(f) covers the information, training, instruction or supervision needed to protect all persons from work risks. (a) is a safe work environment, (c) safe systems of work and (g) health and conditions monitoring.

quiz.question: A university student completes a four-week work placement in Tasman Ridge's credit team. How does the WHS Act treat her?
options: As a visitor, outside the WHS Act's protection
As a worker to whom the bank owes the primary duty
As a worker only if she receives wages from the bank
As the university's responsibility alone
quiz.explanation: Section 7 expressly includes a student gaining work experience as a worker. Payment is not required, and the bank as PCBU owes her the primary duty.

quiz.question: The Act defines 'health' for WHS purposes as:
options: Physical health only
Freedom from notifiable injuries and dangerous incidents
Health as certified by a doctor
Physical and psychological health
quiz.explanation: The WHS Act defines health as physical and psychological health, which is why psychosocial risks fall within the primary duty.

quiz.question: In deciding what is reasonably practicable, when does the cost of a control come into the assessment?
options: First, because controls must fit within the approved safety budget for the year
Never, because cost is irrelevant to WHS duties
After the risk and available controls are assessed, asking whether cost is grossly disproportionate to the risk
Only when a regulator asks for a cost estimate
quiz.explanation: Section 18(e) brings in cost only after assessing the risk and the available controls, and asks whether the cost is grossly disproportionate to the risk.

quiz.question: A branch manager says: 'Our hold-up procedure is on the intranet, so we've met the training duty.' What is the best response?
options: She is right, because making a procedure available always satisfies the training duty under the Act
The duty applies only to head office staff, not branches
Training is only required after a notifiable incident occurs
Section 19(3)(f) asks what training, instruction or supervision is necessary to protect people; posting a document may not be enough
quiz.explanation: The test in s 19(3)(f) is what is necessary to protect people from the risks of the work. Making a document available may not achieve that, especially for high-risk tasks. The duty applies to all workplaces and does not wait for an incident.

quiz.question: Which of these is part of an officer's due diligence under section 27(5)?
options: Personally delivering all WHS training
Approving each individual risk assessment in the bank
Acting as the health and safety representative
Verifying that safety processes are actually used
quiz.explanation: Section 27(5)(f) requires verification of the resources and processes in (c) to (e). Officers need not personally deliver training or approve every assessment, and HSRs are elected by workers.

quiz.question: The bank has not been prosecuted, but an inspector finds the COO took no steps to understand safety risks in the contact centre. Can the COO still be found guilty of breaching the officer duty?
options: No, the bank must be convicted first before any officer can be prosecuted for it
No, officers only owe duties to shareholders and to the board
Yes, an officer can be convicted whether or not the PCBU has been convicted
Yes, but only if the COO is also a director
quiz.explanation: Section 27(4) allows an officer to be convicted of the s 27 duty whether or not the PCBU has been convicted. The officer duty is not limited to directors.

quiz.question: A worker refuses to follow a reasonable, notified instruction to use the sit-stand desk settings set after her ergonomic assessment. Which duty is engaged?
options: The worker's duty to comply, so far as reasonably able, with reasonable instructions
The officer's due diligence duty to verify that resources and processes are used in the workplace
The PCBU's duty to provide welfare facilities
No duty, because ergonomics is outside the WHS Act
quiz.explanation: Section 28(c) requires a worker to comply, so far as they are reasonably able, with reasonable instructions given to allow the PCBU to comply with the Act.

quiz.question: Section 17 tells a duty holder how to manage risks. What is the order it requires?
options: Minimise risks first, then eliminate any that remain after a later review of costs and of available budgets
Insure against risks that cannot be avoided
Transfer risks to contractors where possible
Eliminate risks so far as reasonably practicable; if not reasonably practicable, minimise them
quiz.explanation: Section 17 requires elimination so far as reasonably practicable and, only if that is not reasonably practicable, minimisation so far as reasonably practicable.

sessions.title: Psychosocial hazards, consultation and safety representatives
sessions.summary: See psychosocial hazards as WHS risks, consult workers before changes that affect their health and safety, support health and safety representatives, handle notifiable incidents and protect people who raise concerns.
objectives: Recognise common psychosocial hazards in banking and how to control them
Explain when and how the bank must consult workers and HSRs
Describe HSR training entitlements, the right to cease unsafe work and protection from discriminatory conduct
Apply the notifiable incident steps and record-keeping rule

cards.title: Stage two: the restructure memo
cards.setting: Parramatta contact centre break room, Tuesday, 10:05 am.

lines.text: Stage two. A memo has just landed: the hardship and collections teams will merge, call targets will rise and two team leader roles will go.
People are rattled. Nobody asked us about this. Collections calls are already the hardest calls we take.
Before anyone signs off, we need to look at this the way the WHS Act does. Workload, low control and poor support are hazards too.
It's an efficiency change, not a safety change. Isn't that a management call?
It's both. A change that may affect workers' health or safety is one we have to consult on, and psychological harm counts as harm.
And as HSR I'd like to be part of that conversation before the decision, not after.
Then this stage is about psychosocial hazards, consultation and the people who represent workers. Let's get it right before the memo goes live.

scenes.heading: What they are
scenes.narration: Psychosocial hazards are features of work that can cause psychological harm, and sometimes physical harm too. Examples include high or low job demands, low job control, poor support, unclear roles, poorly managed change and conflict.

scenes.heading: Bullying and harassment
scenes.narration: Workplace bullying, harassment, including sexual harassment, and aggression from customers are psychosocial hazards that banks know well.

scenes.heading: Same duty, same method
scenes.narration: There is no separate 'stress law'. The primary duty already covers psychological health, so the bank manages these risks like any other: eliminate if reasonably practicable, otherwise minimise.

scenes.heading: Regulations and codes
scenes.narration: WHS regulations and codes of practice in many jurisdictions add detail on managing psychosocial risks. Check the current versions where you work.

scenes.heading: Talk to the people doing the work
scenes.narration: Workers and their representatives usually know where the pressure points are. Consultation is not a courtesy here; it is part of the duty.

cards.title: Managing a psychosocial risk
cards.caption: Consultation with workers and HSRs runs through every step, not just the end.

items.label: Identify
items.detail: Look at workload data, complaints, absence, surveys and what workers say

items.label: Assess
items.detail: How long, how often and how severe is the exposure, and who is affected?

items.label: Control
items.detail: Change the work itself first: staffing, targets, call routing, support, role clarity

items.label: Review
items.detail: Check whether controls work, especially after change, incidents or new concerns

cards.question: Which of the following is best described as a psychosocial hazard at a bank?
options: A loose cable across a branch walkway
Sustained high call targets with no time between difficult collections calls
A faulty air-conditioning unit in the server room
An unsecured filing cabinet in the archive
cards.explanation: Sustained high job demands without recovery time is a classic psychosocial hazard. The other options are physical hazards that should also be managed, but they are not psychosocial.

cards.title: Psychosocial or physical?
cards.prompt: Sort each workplace issue into the kind of hazard it mainly presents.

items.text: Repeated abusive calls from customers in arrears
Unclear reporting lines after a merger
Heavy coin bags lifted at the counter
A manager who belittles staff in team meetings
Glare on screens causing eye strain
Restructure rumours with no information for months
Trip hazard from a damaged carpet edge
Working alone in a regional branch with aggressive visitors

cards.title: Consultation, HSRs and the right to speak up about safety
cards.body:
**Consultation (ss 47-49).** The bank must, so far as reasonably practicable, consult workers directly affected by a WHS matter: share relevant information, give them a reasonable chance to have their say, take their views into account and tell them the outcome. It is required when identifying hazards, choosing controls, proposing **changes that may affect health or safety**, and setting procedures, including for **training**.

**Health and safety representatives.** Workers can ask for HSRs to be elected. On an HSR's request, the bank must allow an approved course, pay the fees and give paid time off, as soon as practicable within three months (s 72).

**Stopping unsafe work.** A worker may cease or refuse work if they reasonably fear a serious risk from immediate or imminent exposure to a hazard (s 84).

**No retaliation.** Dismissing or disadvantaging a worker because they are an HSR or raise WHS concerns is prohibited (ss 104-106).

cards.title: The turn: decision first, questions later
cards.setting: Level 12 meeting room, head office, 4:30 pm.

lines.text: The merger plan is final. We'll brief staff on Monday and answer questions then.
James, the plan changes workloads and removes team leaders. That's a change that may affect health and safety. We need to consult before it's locked in.
Collections staff will be taking hardship calls without training on hardship. That's a new risk for them and for customers.
If we consult, won't we be stuck with whatever they want?
No. Consultation means sharing the plan, hearing the concerns, genuinely considering them and telling people what we decided. The bank still decides.

cards.title: Getting the merger right
cards.situation: The merger of hardship and collections teams is due in six weeks. Call targets will rise 15%, two team leader roles go, and collections staff will start taking hardship calls. Ben, as HSR, has asked to be involved. James asks you what to do next.

choices.text: Share the draft plan with affected staff and Ben now, assess the workload and training risks with them, adjust targets, supervision and training where needed, and explain the final decision
choices.outcome: This is consultation as ss 47-49 describe it, done before the change, and it feeds directly into controls such as training under s 19(3)(f).

choices.text: Go ahead as planned and run a staff wellbeing webinar after the merger
choices.outcome: A webinar may help, but it skips consultation on a change that may affect health and safety and does not control the workload risk.

choices.text: Send staff a survey link and implement the plan unchanged, whatever the results
choices.outcome: Asking for views but not taking them into account is not real consultation, and the risks remain unaddressed.

choices.text: Consult only the remaining team leaders, since they will manage the change
choices.outcome: Team leaders matter, but the duty is to consult workers who are directly affected, including the HSR's work group.

cards.title: When a notifiable incident happens
cards.caption: Sections 35-39. Most psychological injuries are not 'notifiable incidents', but they still need reporting internally and managing.

items.label: Recognise it
items.detail: A death, a serious injury or illness, or a dangerous incident arising from the work

items.label: Notify immediately
items.detail: Tell the WHS regulator straight away, by the fastest means, by phone or in writing

items.label: Follow up in writing
items.detail: If the regulator asks after a phone notice, give written notice within 48 hours

items.label: Preserve the site
items.detail: Do not disturb the scene until an inspector arrives or directs, except to help people or make it safe

items.label: Keep the record
items.detail: Keep a record of each notifiable incident for at least five years

cards.back: Person conducting a business or undertaking: for us, the bank. It owes the primary duty of care.
What can reasonably be done, weighing likelihood, harm, knowledge, available controls and finally cost.
A worker elected by a work group to represent them on WHS matters, entitled to approved training.
Sharing information, giving workers a reasonable chance to have a say, taking their views into account and reporting back.
A worker may stop work if reasonably concerned about a serious risk from an immediate or imminent hazard.
Dismissing or disadvantaging someone because they raise WHS issues or hold a WHS role: an offence.

cards.title: Responding when a worker raises a psychosocial concern
cards.prompt: Put the team leader's steps in a sensible order.
steps: Listen, thank the worker and check whether there is any immediate risk to them
Record the concern and tell the worker what will happen next
Gather information and consult the worker, others affected and the HSR
Decide on controls that change the work, not just the person
Put the controls in place and support the worker meanwhile
Review whether the controls worked and report back

cards.question: Ben asks to attend an approved HSR training course. What must the bank do?
options: Allow him to attend as soon as practicable within three months, pay the fees and give paid time off
Allow attendance only if his manager agrees it suits rosters that year
Allow him to attend in his own time, with Ben paying the fees
Offer its own internal course instead of the approved one
cards.explanation: Section 72 requires the PCBU, on the HSR's request, to allow attendance at an approved course the HSR chooses, within three months as soon as practicable, with fees paid and time off with pay.

cards.title: Inside the story: what consultation changed in Parramatta
cards.body:
Leila and Ben ran three short sessions with the affected teams before the merger plan was final. What they heard:

- collections staff had **no training** on hardship requests and feared getting them wrong
- removing both team leaders would leave **no one to escalate** distressing calls to in the evening shift
- the 15% target rise ignored the **longer duration** of hardship calls

**What the bank decided:**
- keep one evening team leader role
- a two-day hardship and difficult-conversations course before anyone takes hardship calls
- targets phased in over three months and measured on quality as well as volume
- a review at 90 days with Ben

The merger went ahead. Staff did not get everything they asked for, but they were heard, the bank recorded why it decided as it did, and the controls changed the work itself. That record is also good evidence of due diligence for James as an officer.

cards.title: Stage two take-aways
items: Psychosocial hazards, such as high demands, low support, poor change management, bullying and harassment, are managed under the same primary duty
Control psychosocial risks by changing the work first, and review controls after change or incidents
Consult affected workers and HSRs before decisions that may affect health and safety, including training procedures
HSRs can request approved training: paid time off and fees, as soon as practicable within three months
Notifiable incidents go to the regulator immediately; keep records for at least five years; never punish someone for raising WHS concerns

cards.prompt: Think about the last significant change in your team, such as new targets, a new system or a restructure. Were the people affected consulted before the decision? What would you do differently next time?

quiz.question: Which of these is a psychosocial hazard?
options: A wet floor near the branch entrance
Exposure to cleaning chemicals stored in the branch kitchen
Poorly managed organisational change
Manual handling of coin boxes
quiz.explanation: Poorly managed change is a recognised psychosocial hazard. The others are physical hazards.

quiz.question: Why does the WHS primary duty cover psychosocial risks?
options: Because a separate stress Act sets those duties
Because the Act defines health to include psychological health
Only because a code of practice says so and the Act itself is silent
Only when a worker makes a compensation claim
quiz.explanation: The WHS Act defines health as physical and psychological health, so the primary duty already extends to psychological harm. Codes and regulations add detail but are not the source of that coverage.

quiz.question: Under section 49, consultation is required when the bank is:
options: Proposing changes that may affect workers' health or safety
Setting the annual dividend
Choosing a new marketing agency
Publishing quarterly financial results
quiz.explanation: Section 49 lists when consultation is required, including proposing changes that may affect health or safety. Dividends, agencies and results are not WHS matters.

quiz.question: Which description best fits consultation under section 48?
options: Telling workers about a decision after it has been made and answering their questions about it
Sharing relevant information, giving workers a reasonable chance to express views, taking them into account and advising the outcome
Obtaining every worker's written agreement before acting
Holding a vote that binds the bank
quiz.explanation: Section 48 describes consultation as information-sharing, a reasonable opportunity to have a say, taking views into account and advising the outcome. It does not require agreement or a binding vote.

quiz.question: A manager plans to move a staff member to a less favourable roster because she was elected HSR and keeps raising issues. What does the WHS Act say?
options: It is allowed if the roster change is temporary and does not reduce her base salary
It is allowed because HSRs have no special protection
It is only a problem if she resigns
This may be discriminatory conduct for a prohibited reason, which the Act forbids
quiz.explanation: Altering a worker's position to their detriment because they are an HSR or raise WHS issues is discriminatory conduct under ss 104-106.

quiz.question: A worker refuses to go into a branch after a credible threat that an armed person is waiting outside. Which provision supports her?
options: The officer's due diligence duty in section 27
The duty to keep notifiable incident records
The right of a worker to cease unsafe work in section 84
The HSR training entitlement in section 72 of the Act, as requested
quiz.explanation: Section 84 lets a worker cease or refuse work where they reasonably fear a serious risk from immediate or imminent exposure to a hazard.

quiz.question: A teller is taken to hospital and admitted as an in-patient after collapsing from a work-related injury. What must the bank do?
options: Notify the regulator within 30 days, once the facts are confirmed by HR
Record it internally only, as it is not notifiable
Wait for the doctor's report before deciding
Notify the WHS regulator immediately by the fastest possible means
quiz.explanation: Immediate treatment as a hospital in-patient makes it a serious injury or illness and so a notifiable incident. Section 38 requires immediate notification by the fastest possible means.

quiz.question: For how long must the bank keep a record of each notifiable incident?
options: At least five years from the date notice is given
Twelve months
Two years from the incident or until the claim closes
Until the injured worker returns to work
quiz.explanation: Section 38(7) requires the PCBU to keep a record of each notifiable incident for at least five years from the day notice is given to the regulator.

quiz.question: Which control for a high-demand contact centre best follows the WHS approach of changing the work first?
options: Giving all staff a resilience webinar and a stress management toolkit
Adding a wellbeing message to payslips
Asking staff to report stress to their GP
Adjusting staffing and call routing to allow recovery time
quiz.explanation: Controls that change the work itself, such as staffing and routing, address the hazard at its source. Individual supports can help but should not replace work-design controls.

quiz.question: Which statement about health and safety representatives is correct?
options: They are appointed by the board to audit managers' safety performance each year
They are elected by workers in a work group to represent them on WHS matters
They replace the bank's duty to consult
They must be qualified safety engineers
quiz.explanation: HSRs are elected by members of a work group. They do not replace consultation with workers and need no professional qualification, though they are entitled to approved training.

sessions.title: The Sex Discrimination Act positive duty
sessions.summary: Understand the section 47C duty to take reasonable and proportionate measures to eliminate sex discrimination, sexual and sex-based harassment, hostile workplace environments and victimisation, and how the Australian Human Rights Commission enforces it.
objectives: Explain who owes the positive duty and what conduct it targets
Apply the duty to harassment by colleagues and by customers
Judge what reasonable and proportionate measures look like for a bank
Describe the Commission's inquiry, compliance notice and enforcement powers

cards.title: Stage three: 'it's just banter'
cards.setting: Tasman Ridge Bank branch, Elizabeth Street, Hobart. Friday, 3:50 pm.

lines.text: Stage three. Chloe has called you and Leila from Hobart. A young teller, Mia, has asked to be moved off the Friday roster.
One of our biggest business customers comes in every Friday. He comments on Mia's looks, asks if she's single, and last week he said women shouldn't be lending money.
And a senior lender in my team laughs along and repeats the jokes in the lunch room. Mia hasn't made a formal complaint. She just wants to avoid Fridays.
So the conduct comes from a customer and from our own staff, and nobody has complained formally. Under the old way of thinking we'd wait. Under the positive duty we can't.
If Mia does complain later, we also need to make sure nobody treats her worse for it. That's victimisation, and it is covered too.
This stage is about section 47C of the Sex Discrimination Act: the duty to prevent, not just respond.

scenes.heading: A duty to prevent
scenes.narration: Employers and PCBUs must take reasonable and proportionate measures to eliminate, as far as possible, certain unlawful conduct. It is a proactive duty: it applies even when no one has complained.

scenes.heading: What it targets
scenes.narration: Sex discrimination in employment, sexual harassment, harassment on the ground of sex, conduct creating a workplace environment hostile on the ground of sex, and victimisation linked to complaints about those things.

scenes.heading: Whose conduct
scenes.narration: The duty covers conduct by the bank itself, its employees or workers, and its agents. It also covers harassment and hostile conduct by third parties, such as customers, towards the bank's employees and workers.

scenes.heading: What is reasonable
scenes.narration: Whether measures are enough depends on the size, nature and circumstances of the business, its resources, and the practicability and cost of measures. A large bank is expected to do a lot.

scenes.heading: Alongside WHS
scenes.narration: Section 47C does not limit WHS duties. Sexual harassment is both a positive-duty issue and a psychosocial hazard, so the two frameworks work together.

cards.title: Reacting to complaints versus the positive duty
cards.caption: Complaint handling still matters, but the positive duty asks what the bank does before anyone complains.

items.label: Trigger
items.right: Applies all the time, complaint or not

items.label: Third parties
items.left: Customers often treated as outside scope
items.right: Customer harassment of staff is covered

items.label: Evidence
items.right: Risk assessments, measures, training, monitoring, outcomes

cards.question: No one in Hobart has lodged a complaint about the Friday customer. Does the positive duty still require the bank to act?
options: No, the duty is triggered only by a formal complaint
Only if the customer's conduct is reported to police
Yes, the duty requires reasonable and proportionate measures to eliminate such conduct as far as possible, with or without a complaint
No, conduct by customers is outside the Sex Discrimination Act
cards.explanation: Section 47C is a proactive duty. It covers sexual harassment and sex-based harassment of employees by any person, including customers, under s 47C(4), and does not depend on a complaint.

cards.title: Name the conduct
cards.prompt: Match each type of conduct covered by the positive duty to a description in plain words.

pairs.right: Unwelcome conduct of a sexual nature that a reasonable person would anticipate could offend, humiliate or intimidate

pairs.left: Harassment on the ground of sex
pairs.right: Unwelcome demeaning conduct because of a person's sex or characteristics linked to it
Conduct that makes a workplace offensive, intimidating or humiliating for people of a particular sex
Treating someone badly because they complained, or might complain, about unlawful conduct
Treating someone less favourably in hiring, pay, promotion or dismissal because of their sex

cards.title: How the Commission enforces the positive duty
cards.body:
The **Australian Human Rights Commission Act 1986** gives the Commission specific functions for the positive duty (s 35A):

- publish **guidelines** on complying with the duty, and promote understanding of it
- run research and education programs
- **inquire** into an organisation's compliance where it reasonably suspects non-compliance (s 35B), giving written notice and a chance to make submissions
- notify findings and recommendations
- issue a **compliance notice** specifying action to take, with a period starting at least 21 days after the notice (s 35F)
- apply to the Federal Court or the Federal Circuit and Family Court to enforce a notice that is not complied with (s 35J)

The Commission's guidelines describe what compliance looks like in practice, including leadership, risk management, support, reporting and training. They are not law in themselves, but they are the best guide to what the regulator will expect from a bank of our size.

cards.title: The turn: 'he's one of our best customers'
cards.setting: Hobart branch manager's office, Monday, 9:10 am.

lines.text: The relationship manager says if we confront him, he'll take his business accounts elsewhere.
The positive duty doesn't have a customer-value exception. His conduct towards Mia is exactly what s 47C(4) covers.
And the lender laughing along and repeating it? That's our own employee contributing to a hostile environment.
What does 'reasonable and proportionate' look like for a bank our size?
More than a poster. We need measures that actually change what happens in that branch on a Friday, and in every branch like it.

cards.title: Fixing Fridays in Hobart
cards.situation: You must recommend what Tasman Ridge does about the Friday customer and the lender who repeats his jokes. Mia has not complained formally and is worried about being seen as a troublemaker.

choices.text: Remove Mia from Friday rosters and take no further action, as she asked
choices.outcome: This protects Mia in the short term, but it shifts the burden onto her and leaves the conduct and environment unchanged for everyone else.

choices.text: Have a senior person set conditions for the customer's service, deal with the lender through the conduct process, check in with Mia confidentially, and review customer-harassment controls in all branches
choices.outcome: This acts on both sources of conduct, supports Mia without making her responsible, guards against victimisation and treats it as a system risk. It reflects the preventive purpose of s 47C.

choices.text: Wait until Mia makes a formal written complaint, then investigate
choices.outcome: The positive duty does not wait for a complaint. Waiting allows the harassment and hostile environment to continue.

choices.text: Send all Hobart staff a reminder of the anti-harassment policy
choices.outcome: A reminder alone is unlikely to be a reasonable and proportionate measure for a known, continuing problem.

cards.title: Building blocks of prevention
cards.caption: Our own framework for organising measures. Check the Commission's current guidelines for its expectations.

items.label: Leadership
items.detail: Leaders set expectations, model behaviour and are held accountable

items.label: Risk assessment
items.detail: Identify where harassment risks arise: customers, events, power imbalances, isolated work

items.label: Controls and training
items.detail: Clear rules, practical training for all, deeper training for managers

items.label: Support and reporting
items.detail: Several safe ways to raise concerns, with confidentiality and no victimisation

items.label: Monitoring
items.detail: Track data, check whether measures work and improve them

cards.title: Prevention or reaction?
cards.prompt: Sort each action by whether it mainly prevents conduct or mainly reacts after it happens.

items.text: Assessing harassment risks before the end-of-year function
Investigating a complaint received last week
Practical training for managers on stepping in early
Setting service conditions for customers who harass staff
Disciplining a lender after an investigation
Tracking harassment data by branch to spot hot spots
Paying compensation after a tribunal finding
Rostering so no one works alone with known problem customers

cards.question: Which matter is relevant under s 47C(6) when deciding whether the bank's measures are reasonable and proportionate?
options: Whether the harasser is a valuable customer
The size, nature and circumstances of the business and its resources
Whether the affected employee is permanent or casual
Whether any complaint has been made to the Commission
cards.explanation: Section 47C(6) lists the size, nature and circumstances of the business, its resources, the practicability and cost of measures, and any other relevant matter. A customer's commercial value is not a reason to do less.

cards.title: Inside the story: the end-of-year function
cards.body:
Tasman Ridge's Sydney end-of-year party had a history: an open bar, no end time and senior staff 'running the after-party'. Two informal concerns were raised the previous year, but nobody complained formally.

**Leila's prevention plan, approved by James:**
- a risk assessment of the event with the people and culture team and an HSR
- a clear end time, food throughout, and no bank-funded after-party
- named senior **'event leads'** briefed on stepping in early and on how to escalate
- a reminder to all staff of expected behaviour and of the confidential ways to raise concerns, including Aroha's team
- a check-in survey a week later

**Why it matters:** the earlier informal concerns meant the risk was known. Under s 47C the question is not only whether someone complained, but whether the bank took reasonable and proportionate measures to stop it happening again.

cards.title: Stage three take-aways
items: Section 47C requires reasonable and proportionate measures to eliminate, as far as possible, sex discrimination, sexual and sex-based harassment, hostile workplace environments and related victimisation
The duty is proactive: it applies whether or not anyone has complained
It covers conduct by the bank, its workers and agents, and harassment of staff by third parties such as customers
What is reasonable depends on size, nature, resources and practicability; a large bank is expected to do more
The Commission can inquire, issue compliance notices and seek court enforcement; s 47C works alongside WHS duties

cards.prompt: Where in your workplace are staff most exposed to sexual or sex-based harassment: customers, events, travel, isolated work or power imbalances? What one preventive measure would make the biggest difference there?

quiz.question: In which Act is the positive duty to eliminate sexual harassment found?
options: Work Health and Safety Act 2011, section 19
Sex Discrimination Act 1984, section 47C
Corporations Act 2001, section 1317AI
Fair Work Act 2009, section 47C
quiz.explanation: The positive duty is in s 47C of the Sex Discrimination Act 1984. It sits alongside, and does not limit, WHS duties.

quiz.question: What standard does section 47C set for the measures an employer must take?
options: Reasonable and proportionate measures to eliminate the conduct as far as possible
Every measure needed to guarantee that no harassment ever occurs anywhere in the business
Measures listed in a schedule to the Act
Measures agreed with a union
quiz.explanation: Section 47C(1) requires reasonable and proportionate measures to eliminate the relevant conduct, as far as possible. It is not an absolute guarantee or a fixed list.

quiz.question: Which of these conduct types is within the positive duty?
options: Conduct creating a workplace environment hostile on the ground of sex
A customer's complaint about a fee
Underpayment of overtime unrelated to sex
A dispute about parking spaces
quiz.explanation: Section 47C(2)(c) and (4)(b) cover hostile workplace environment conduct under s 28M. The other options are not sex-based conduct.

quiz.question: A customer repeatedly makes sexual comments to a teller. Is this within the bank's positive duty?
options: No, only conduct by the bank's own employees and agents is covered by the duty towards them
Only if the customer is also an employee of another bank
Yes, sexual harassment of employees by any person, including customers, is covered
Only if the teller reports it to police
quiz.explanation: Section 47C(4) covers sexual harassment and sex-based harassment of the duty holder's employees or workers by third parties, which includes customers.

quiz.question: After Mia complains, her manager stops offering her overtime. Which conduct covered by the positive duty may this be?
options: A hostile workplace environment only
Victimisation related to a complaint
Indirect discrimination on the ground of age
A personal work-related grievance excluded by the Act
quiz.explanation: Section 47C(2)(d) and (4)(c) cover victimisation linked to complaints or allegations about the covered conduct. Penalising someone for complaining is the classic example.

quiz.question: Which body can inquire into an employer's compliance with the positive duty and issue a compliance notice?
options: The Human Rights Commission
ASIC
APRA
The Fair Work Ombudsman's office
quiz.explanation: The AHRC Act gives the Australian Human Rights Commission functions to inquire into compliance with the positive duty and, through its President, to issue compliance notices.

quiz.question: A compliance notice under the AHRC Act must give the organisation how long to take the specified action?
options: A reasonable period starting at least 21 days after the notice is given
Seven days from receipt of the notice
Exactly 90 days, in every case, whatever the action required from the date of the finding
Whatever period the employer proposes
quiz.explanation: Section 35F(2)(d) requires a reasonable period starting at least 21 days after the notice is given.

quiz.question: What happens if an organisation does not comply with a compliance notice?
options: The Commission may cancel the organisation's business registration and trading licence immediately
ASIC automatically issues an infringement notice with a penalty for each day of delay
Nothing, because compliance notices are advisory only
The President may apply to the Federal Court or Federal Circuit and Family Court for an order
quiz.explanation: Section 35J allows the President to apply to the court for an order where a person has not complied with a compliance notice that is not under reconsideration or review.

quiz.question: How does section 47C relate to WHS duties?
options: It does not limit duties under WHS laws; both apply
It replaces WHS duties for harassment matters and complaints at the bank
WHS laws no longer apply to sexual harassment
It applies only where no WHS law exists
quiz.explanation: Section 47C(7) says the positive duty does not limit or affect duties under the Commonwealth WHS Act or state and territory WHS laws.

quiz.question: Which measure is most clearly preventive rather than reactive?
options: Investigating a complaint thoroughly after a staff event has finished
Disciplining an employee after a finding
Assessing harassment risks before a staff event and setting controls
Settling a claim with a former employee
quiz.explanation: The positive duty focuses on preventing conduct. A risk assessment with controls before an event is preventive; the others respond after harm.

sessions.title: Whistleblower protections under Corporations Act Part 9.4AAA
sessions.summary: Learn who is an eligible whistleblower, what can be disclosed and to whom, the confidentiality and immunity protections, the ban on victimisation, and the lessons of ASIC's first whistleblower enforcement outcome.
objectives: Decide whether a disclosure qualifies for protection
Distinguish disclosable matters from personal work-related grievances
Apply the confidentiality rules when handling and investigating a disclosure
Recognise victimisation, including threats and reputational harm, and its consequences

cards.title: Stage four: 'just tell me who it was'
cards.setting: Whistleblower protection office, head office, Sydney. Wednesday, 11:20 am.

lines.text: Stage four. Aroha has received a disclosure through the bank's speak-up platform, made anonymously.
Someone in business lending says income figures in loan files are being changed so applications pass credit policy. They attached two before-and-after screenshots.
That's serious. The business lending head has already called me. He wants to know who sent it so he can 'clear the air'.
He can't have that, and neither can you, unless the discloser consents. Telling him, or giving hints that point to them, could itself be a contravention.
And if he starts moving people off the team because he suspects them, that could be victimisation even if he guesses wrong.
This stage is Part 9.4AAA of the Corporations Act: who is protected, what they can report, to whom, and what we must never do.

scenes.heading: Banks are covered
scenes.narration: The whistleblower protections apply to regulated entities, which include companies and every authorised deposit-taking institution and its subsidiaries.

scenes.heading: Who is protected
scenes.narration: Eligible whistleblowers include current and former officers and employees, suppliers of goods or services and their employees, associates, and relatives or dependants of any of them.

scenes.heading: What they can report
scenes.narration: Information they have reasonable grounds to suspect concerns misconduct or an improper state of affairs, including breaches of laws such as the Corporations Act, Banking Act, credit law and FAR, serious Commonwealth offences, or dangers to the public or the financial system.

scenes.heading: Who can receive it
scenes.narration: ASIC, APRA, and eligible recipients inside the bank, such as officers, senior managers, auditors, actuaries and people the bank authorises. Disclosures to a lawyer for advice on these protections are protected too.

scenes.heading: Anonymous is fine
scenes.narration: A whistleblower does not have to give their name. Anonymous disclosures can still qualify for protection.

cards.title: Does a disclosure qualify for protection?
cards.caption: Based on ss 1317AA-1317AADA. The discloser needs reasonable grounds to suspect, not proof.

items.label: Eligible whistleblower?
items.detail: Current or former officer, employee, supplier, associate, or their relative or dependant

items.label: Right recipient?
items.detail: ASIC, APRA, an eligible recipient, or a lawyer for advice on the protections

items.label: Reasonable grounds?
items.detail: Reasonable grounds to suspect misconduct, an improper state of affairs or a listed contravention

items.label: Not only a personal grievance?
items.detail: Solely personal work-related grievances are excluded unless they involve victimisation

items.label: Protected
items.detail: Confidentiality, immunity and protection from detriment apply

cards.question: The anonymous discloser in business lending turns out to be a former contractor whose engagement ended last month. Can the disclosure still qualify for protection?
options: No, only current employees are eligible whistleblowers
No, anonymous disclosures never qualify
Only if the contractor first reported it to a manager
Yes, former suppliers of services and their employees can be eligible whistleblowers
cards.explanation: Section 1317AAA covers anyone who is or has been an officer, employee, supplier of goods or services, or an employee of a supplier. Anonymity does not prevent protection, and there is no need to go through a manager first.

cards.title: Protected disclosure or personal grievance?
cards.prompt: Sort each report by how Part 9.4AAA is likely to treat it.

items.text: Income figures in loan files changed to pass credit policy
I was not promoted and I think the decision was unfair to me
Fees charged to customers that the product terms do not allow
A clash with my team leader about my desk location
Risk reports to the board misstate known AML breaches
I disagree with my performance rating this year
After I reported misconduct, my shifts were cut
Systems failures that could endanger the financial system

cards.title: What the protections actually do
cards.body:
**Confidentiality (s 1317AAE).** No one may disclose the whistleblower's identity, or information likely to identify them, obtained because of the disclosure, unless an exception applies: to ASIC, APRA or the AFP, to a lawyer for advice, or with the discloser's **consent**. Other information may be shared if reasonably necessary to investigate, with all reasonable steps taken to reduce the risk of identification. Breach is an offence and a civil penalty provision.

**Immunity (s 1317AB).** No civil, criminal or administrative liability, including discipline, for making the disclosure, plus qualified privilege. Their own misconduct is not excused.

**No victimisation (s 1317AC).** It is unlawful to cause or threaten detriment because someone made, or might make, a protected disclosure. Detriment includes dismissal, harassment, psychological harm and reputational damage.

**Remedies (ss 1317AD-1317AE).** Courts can order compensation and other remedies. Once the applicant points to a reasonable possibility of detriment, the other side must prove the claim is not made out.

lines.text: James, I've just heard the business lending head plans to move two analysts to the back office 'for their own development'. Both had access to those files.
He says it's unrelated. The timing is awkward, I admit.
Under s 1317AC, it doesn't matter whether he's right about who reported. If his suspicion is part of the reason, that's victimisation.
And moving people off a team against their wishes, right after a disclosure, will look exactly like detriment to anyone reviewing it later.

cards.title: Protecting the discloser while investigating
cards.situation: The disclosure about altered loan files is credible. The business lending head is pressing for names and planning a reshuffle. You must advise James, as the accountable executive, on the next steps.

choices.text: Pause the reshuffle, remind the business lending head in writing of the confidentiality and victimisation rules, appoint an independent investigator, share only what is needed and watch for detriment
choices.outcome: This protects confidentiality, prevents detriment, keeps the investigation independent and creates a record. It reflects what ss 1317AAE and 1317AC require.

choices.text: Let the business lending head run the investigation, since he knows the files best
choices.outcome: He is conflicted and has already sought the discloser's identity. This risks both identification and detriment.

choices.text: Allow the reshuffle but ask HR to document that it is for development
choices.outcome: Paperwork does not change the reason. If suspicion of a disclosure is part of the reason, the move may still be victimisation.

choices.text: Pause the reshuffle but tell the business lending head who reported, so he can be careful around them
choices.outcome: Pausing helps, but disclosing identity without consent is itself a contravention, and makes detriment more likely.

cards.title: Whistleblowing in numbers: what ASIC has found
cards.caption: Sources: ASIC media releases 25-179MR (27 August 2025) and 25-294MR (4 December 2025).

items.label: TerraCom penalty
items.detail: Federal Court penalty in 2025 for whistleblower victimisation: ASIC's first enforcement outcome on these provisions

items.label: Entities surveyed
items.detail: ASIC's 2024-25 whistleblower questionnaire, across 18 industries (REP 827, published December 2025)

items.label: No dedicated web page
items.detail: Participating entities without a dedicated whistleblower web page for raising concerns

items.label: No regular training
items.detail: Participating entities that did not provide regular staff training on their whistleblower program

items.label: No employee feedback
items.detail: Had not sought employee feedback on their whistleblower program in the past year

cards.title: Real case: ASIC v TerraCom (Federal Court, 2025)
cards.body:
**What happened.** TerraCom, an ASX-listed mining company, made two ASX announcements and published an open letter to shareholders in 2020 saying a whistleblower's allegations were false and that it had had its employees' conduct independently investigated.

**The outcome.** In August 2025 the Federal Court ordered TerraCom to pay a **AUD 7.5 million** penalty for whistleblower victimisation, plus AUD 1 million of ASIC's costs. TerraCom admitted the statements caused the whistleblower hurt, humiliation and distress and damaged his reputation, when an independent investigation had at least partly supported his allegations. ASIC said it was its first enforcement outcome for the whistleblower provisions. Separate claims against individual directors and officers were dismissed.

**The lesson for a bank.** Detriment is not only dismissal. Public statements, even when meant to reassure markets, can harm a whistleblower's reputation and breach s 1317AC. Communications about a disclosure need the same care as the investigation itself.

cards.back: Inside the bank: an officer, senior manager, auditor, actuary or a person authorised to receive disclosures.
To a journalist or parliamentarian, only after a disclosure to ASIC, APRA or a prescribed body, at least 90 days passing, written notice and other conditions.
To a journalist or parliamentarian after an earlier regulator disclosure, where there is a substantial and imminent danger to health, safety or the environment, after written notice.
A grievance about one's own employment with personal implications only; excluded unless it involves victimisation or wider misconduct.
Includes dismissal, demotion, discrimination, harassment, psychological harm and damage to reputation or finances.
Protection the discloser has for the disclosure, for example against a defamation claim.

cards.question: A senior manager receives a protected disclosure and wants to brief the investigator. Which approach is consistent with s 1317AAE?
options: Share the discloser's name with the investigator and the business lending head
Share no information at all, so the matter cannot be investigated
Share the information reasonably necessary to investigate, without the discloser's identity, and take reasonable steps to reduce the risk of identification
Share the identity only with people who promise to keep it confidential
cards.explanation: Section 1317AAE(4) allows disclosure of information other than identity where reasonably necessary to investigate, if all reasonable steps are taken to reduce the risk of identification. Identity itself needs consent or another listed exception.

cards.title: If someone brings you a concern
cards.body:
You may be an **eligible recipient** without realising it: officers and senior managers are. If a colleague raises a possible misconduct concern with you:

- thank them and do not ask them to prove it
- do not share their identity, or clues to it, with anyone, without their consent
- tell them about the whistleblower policy and protections
- pass the matter to the whistleblower protection officer in the way the policy sets out
- never treat them differently because they spoke up

cards.title: Stage four take-aways
items: Part 9.4AAA protects eligible whistleblowers, including former staff, suppliers and their relatives, who disclose to ASIC, APRA, eligible recipients or a lawyer
Disclosable matters need reasonable grounds to suspect misconduct, an improper state of affairs or a listed contravention; solely personal work-related grievances are excluded
Identity, and information likely to identify a whistleblower, must stay confidential except with consent or a listed exception
Causing or threatening detriment because of a suspected disclosure is unlawful, even if the suspicion is wrong
ASIC v TerraCom (2025) showed that public statements can be detriment, with a AUD 7.5 million penalty

cards.prompt: If a colleague told you tomorrow that they suspected misconduct in your area, what would you say in the first two minutes, and who would you pass it to?

quiz.question: Which Part of the Corporations Act contains the corporate sector whistleblower protections?
options: Part 9.4AAA
Part 7.7A (Division 2)
Part 2D.1
Part 9.4B
quiz.explanation: Part 9.4AAA contains the whistleblower protections. Part 7.7A deals with advice, Part 2D.1 with officers' duties, and Part 9.4B with civil penalty proceedings.

quiz.question: Which person is an eligible whistleblower in relation to Tasman Ridge Bank?
options: A member of the public with no link to the bank
The spouse of a current bank employee
A journalist who heard a rumour
A competitor bank's employee with no dealings with the bank
quiz.explanation: Section 1317AAA includes relatives and dependants of officers, employees and suppliers. People with no connection to the bank are not eligible whistleblowers.

quiz.question: Which of these is an eligible recipient within the bank?
options: Any customer of the bank
A teller's family member
A senior manager of the bank
A journalist covering banking
quiz.explanation: Section 1317AAC lists officers, senior managers, auditors, actuaries and authorised persons of the body corporate or a related body corporate.

quiz.question: What state of mind must a discloser have about the information for it to be a disclosable matter?
options: Proof beyond reasonable doubt that the conduct occurred, supported by documents and emails
Reasonable grounds to suspect it concerns misconduct or an improper state of affairs
A signed statement from a witness and the bank's general counsel
Certainty that a criminal offence occurred
quiz.explanation: Section 1317AA(4) and (5) require reasonable grounds to suspect. Proof or certainty is not required.

quiz.question: An employee reports only that her request for a transfer was refused and she feels it was unfair to her. How is this most likely treated?
options: As a protected disclosure in every case
As a personal work-related grievance outside the protections, unless it involves victimisation or wider misconduct
As a public interest disclosure
As a notifiable incident under the WHS Act
quiz.explanation: Section 1317AADA excludes personal work-related grievances, such as decisions about transfer, unless they have significant wider implications, involve listed conduct or concern victimisation.

quiz.question: Which of the following is an exception that allows the whistleblower's identity to be disclosed?
options: Disclosure to the business unit head so he can be careful
Disclosure to the board's chair as a courtesy
Disclosure to the alleged wrongdoer for a fair response
Disclosure with the whistleblower's consent
quiz.explanation: Section 1317AAE(2) allows identity to be disclosed to ASIC, APRA, the AFP, a lawyer for advice, a prescribed body, or with consent. Internal courtesy briefings are not exceptions.

quiz.question: A manager wrongly suspects an analyst made a disclosure and cuts her shifts for that reason. Has he contravened s 1317AC?
options: No, because she did not actually make the disclosure
No, because cutting shifts is not dismissal
Yes, detriment caused because of a belief or suspicion about a disclosure is victimisation even if the belief is wrong
Only if she can prove the disclosure was true
quiz.explanation: Section 1317AC(1) applies where the person believes or suspects that someone made, may have made or could make a qualifying disclosure, and that is part of the reason. Detriment is broadly defined.

quiz.question: Before making a public interest disclosure to a journalist, what must generally have happened?
options: A disclosure to the bank's CEO and a 30-day wait
Approval from ASIC to go public
A previous qualifying disclosure to ASIC, APRA or a prescribed body, at least 90 days passing, and written notice to that body
Nothing; journalists are always eligible recipients
quiz.explanation: Section 1317AAD(1) requires an earlier disclosure under s 1317AA(1), at least 90 days, no reasonable grounds to believe action is being taken, a public interest belief, and written notice, among other conditions.

quiz.question: In ASIC v TerraCom, what conduct led to the 2025 victimisation penalty?
options: Dismissing the whistleblower on the day he reported and then withholding his final pay and leave
Refusing to have a whistleblower policy
Public announcements and an open letter saying the whistleblower's allegations were false
Failing to report the disclosure to APRA within the time the law requires
quiz.explanation: The case concerned two ASX announcements and an open letter in 2020 stating the allegations were false. TerraCom admitted they caused detriment, including reputational damage.

quiz.question: In a claim for compensation for victimisation, what happens once the applicant points to evidence suggesting a reasonable possibility of the detrimental conduct?
options: The applicant must then prove the claim beyond reasonable doubt, with written evidence
The claim is automatically successful
ASIC must take over the proceedings
The other party bears the onus of proving the claim is not made out
quiz.explanation: Section 1317AD(2B) shifts the onus: once the applicant adduces or points to evidence of a reasonable possibility, the respondent must prove the claim is not made out.

sessions.title: Accountability under FAR and assessment readiness
sessions.summary: Connect the Financial Accountability Regime, whistleblower policies and WHS officer duties into one people-safety program with clear accountability, role-based training and evidence the board and regulators can rely on.
objectives: Describe FAR's accountable persons and their accountability obligations
Explain deferred remuneration, key personnel and disqualification under FAR
List what a whistleblower policy must contain and the training ASIC expects
Assemble evidence of a working people-safety program for the board

cards.title: Stage five: the board wants evidence
cards.setting: Board risk committee pre-meeting, Level 30, head office, Sydney. Monday, 7:45 am.

lines.text: Final stage. The board risk committee meets on Thursday. Its chair has asked one question: 'Show us that our people are safe, heard and protected, and who is accountable.'
As COO I'm a registered accountable person under FAR. Operations, including people safety in the contact centres, sits in my accountability statement.
So Thursday isn't just a WHS update. It's evidence that you've taken reasonable steps in your accountability, and that officers have exercised due diligence.
The whistleblower program needs to be in the pack too. Policy, channels, training, cases, and how we protect people.
And the HSRs' view. If the board only hears from managers, they'll miss half the picture.
Hobart is ready to show what we changed on Fridays.
Then let's build the pack, and make sure you're ready for the final exam at the same time.

cards.title: The Financial Accountability Regime in brief

scenes.heading: Two regulators, one regime
scenes.narration: The Financial Accountability Regime, FAR, is administered jointly by APRA and ASIC. It replaced the Banking Executive Accountability Regime and has applied to banks and their holding companies since 15 March 2024.

scenes.heading: Accountable persons
scenes.narration: An accountable person is someone with actual or effective senior executive responsibility for managing the bank, or a significant part of it, plus people in roles or responsibilities the rules prescribe. Banks must register them.

scenes.heading: Accountability obligations
scenes.narration: Accountable persons must act with honesty and integrity and with due skill, care and diligence, deal with the regulators openly and cooperatively, and take reasonable steps to prevent matters that would damage the bank's prudential standing or reputation, or cause material breaches of key financial laws.

scenes.heading: Statements and maps
scenes.narration: The bank gives the regulator accountability statements for each accountable person and an accountability map showing who is responsible for what, so nothing important falls between the cracks.

scenes.heading: Pay with consequences
scenes.narration: A portion of each accountable person's variable pay must be deferred, and the bank's remuneration policy must reduce it for failures to meet their obligations. The regulator can also disqualify a person.

cards.title: FAR obligations: the bank and the person
cards.caption: From the Financial Accountability Regime Act 2023. The key law list in s 21 includes the Banking Act, credit legislation and financial services law.

items.label: Honesty and care
items.left: Take reasonable steps to conduct business with honesty, integrity, skill, care and diligence
items.right: Act with honesty, integrity, skill, care and diligence in the role

items.label: Regulators
items.left: Take reasonable steps to deal with APRA and ASIC openly and cooperatively
items.right: Deal with APRA and ASIC openly and cooperatively

items.label: Prevention
items.left: Take reasonable steps to prevent damage to prudential standing or reputation
items.right: Take reasonable steps to prevent such damage and material breaches of key laws

items.label: Oversight
items.left: Make sure accountable persons and significant related entities comply
items.right: Own the responsibilities in their accountability statement

cards.question: Under FAR, what must a bank's remuneration policy provide for an accountable person who fails to meet their accountability obligations?
options: Their variable remuneration is reduced by an amount proportionate to the failure
Their fixed salary is frozen for one year
Their bonus is paid to the whistleblower who reported the failure
Nothing, because remuneration is outside FAR
cards.explanation: Section 25(1)(b) of the FAR Act requires a remuneration policy under which variable remuneration is reduced proportionately to the failure, and the reduction can be to zero.

cards.title: FAR's four obligation sets
cards.prompt: Match each set of obligations of an accountable entity to what it requires.

pairs.right: Conduct business honestly and with due care, cooperate with regulators and prevent prudential harm
Make sure accountable persons together cover every part of the group's operations
Defer part of accountable persons' variable pay and reduce it for failures
Give the regulator accountability statements, the accountability map and notice of key events

cards.title: Real case: APRA's prudential inquiry into CBA (2018)
cards.body:
**Background.** In August 2017 APRA set up a prudential inquiry into governance, culture and accountability at the Commonwealth Bank of Australia after a series of incidents that damaged its reputation. The final report was released on 1 May 2018.

**What the panel found.** CBA's financial success had dulled its senses to warning signs, particularly for operational, compliance and conduct risk. The panel pointed to **unclear accountabilities**, weak escalation of issues, slow and overly collegial decision-making, an under-resourced compliance function, and pay that, for senior managers, had **little sting** when risk or customer outcomes were poor.

**The response.** CBA gave APRA an enforceable undertaking to fix the issues, and APRA applied a AUD 1 billion add-on to its minimum capital requirement.

**The lesson.** People-related risks, such as conduct, speak-up culture and safety, are non-financial risks. FAR's clear accountabilities and remuneration consequences grew from lessons like these.

cards.title: The turn: is the whistleblower policy enough?

lines.text: Our policy covers everything the Act lists. But when I asked ten people in Parramatta where to raise a concern, four didn't know the policy existed.
The contact centre induction covers WHS and harassment. Whistleblowing is a link at the end that nobody clicks.
A policy on the intranet meets the 'make it available' requirement. Whether it works is a different question.
And ASIC's own reviews keep finding the same gap: no regular training. I don't want our name on that list.

cards.title: Whistleblower policies and the training ASIC expects
cards.body:
**The legal requirement (s 1317AI).** A public company, and a large proprietary company, must have a whistleblower policy and make it available to its officers and employees. The policy must explain:

- the protections available to whistleblowers
- to whom disclosures can be made, and how
- how the company will support whistleblowers and protect them from detriment
- how it will investigate disclosures
- how it will ensure fair treatment of employees mentioned in disclosures
- how the policy is made available

Failing to have one is a strict liability offence.

**ASIC's guidance (RG 270).** ASIC expects upfront and ongoing education and training on the policy for all staff, appropriate training for managers, and **specialist training for eligible recipients** and others with roles in handling disclosures. Training is guidance rather than an express statutory duty, but it is how a bank shows its policy actually works.

cards.title: What goes in the board pack?
cards.situation: The board risk committee wants evidence that people are safe, heard and protected. You have one page for the summary. Which approach do you recommend to Leila and James?

choices.text: List all policies with their approval dates
choices.outcome: Approved policies matter, but they do not show whether risks are controlled, training happens or people are protected in practice.

choices.text: Show key risks and controls, role-based training and its effectiveness, HSR consultation, harassment prevention outcomes, de-identified whistleblower metrics, open actions and who is accountable
choices.outcome: This gives the board evidence of controls, verification and accountability across WHS, the positive duty and Part 9.4AAA, mapped to accountable persons.

choices.text: Report the number of whistleblower disclosures with the names of the business units and disclosers involved
choices.outcome: Disclosure metrics help, but naming disclosers, or details that identify them, would breach confidentiality.

choices.text: Show training completion rates only, since they are easy to measure
choices.outcome: Completion is a useful start, but it does not show whether training was suitable or controls worked.
