cards.title: Building the annual people-safety assurance cycle
cards.prompt: Put the steps of Tasman Ridge's annual cycle in a sensible order.
steps: Map each obligation (WHS, positive duty, whistleblowing) to an accountable person and an owner
Assess the risks with workers and HSRs, including psychosocial and harassment risks
Set controls and role-based training: all staff, managers, HSRs and eligible recipients
Deliver training and record attendance and assessment results
Test effectiveness through audits, surveys, incident and disclosure data
Report to the board risk committee and fix the gaps found

cards.question: Which statement about Tasman Ridge's whistleblower policy is correct?
options: It must be lodged with ASIC before it takes effect
It is optional for banks that have a speak-up platform
It only needs to cover disclosures made to ASIC and APRA
As a public company, the bank must have a policy covering the matters in s 1317AI(5) and make it available to officers and employees
cards.explanation: Section 1317AI requires public companies to have a policy covering the listed matters and to make it available to officers and employees. There is no lodgement requirement, and a platform does not replace the policy.

cards.title: Stage five take-aways
items: FAR, run jointly by APRA and ASIC, has applied to banks since 15 March 2024 and replaced BEAR
Accountable persons must act with honesty, integrity, skill, care and diligence, cooperate with regulators and take reasonable steps to prevent prudential harm and material breaches
Part of accountable persons' variable pay is deferred and must be reduced for failures; the regulator can disqualify
Public companies must have and make available a whistleblower policy; ASIC expects ongoing training, with specialist training for eligible recipients
Evidence that works joins it all up: risks, controls, role-based training, consultation, outcomes and named accountability

cards.prompt: If your board asked tomorrow for evidence that people in your area are safe, heard and protected, what three pieces of evidence could you produce, and what is missing?

quiz.question: Which regulators jointly administer the Financial Accountability Regime?
options: AUSTRAC and ASIC
APRA and the Reserve Bank
APRA and ASIC
ASIC and the AHRC
quiz.explanation: FAR is jointly administered by APRA and ASIC, as both regulators' official pages state.

quiz.question: From what date has FAR applied to authorised deposit-taking institutions?
options: 1 July 2018
15 March 2024
1 January 2020
15 March 2025
quiz.explanation: FAR commenced for ADIs and their authorised NOHCs on 15 March 2024; insurers and super trustees followed from 15 March 2025.

quiz.question: Which regime did FAR replace?
options: The Banking Code of Practice as it applied before 2025
The Corporations Act whistleblower regime
Prudential Standard CPS 520
The Banking Executive Accountability Regime (BEAR)
quiz.explanation: APRA and ASIC both describe FAR as replacing BEAR, which commenced in 2018.

quiz.question: Which is an accountability obligation of an accountable person under s 21 of the FAR Act?
options: Dealing with APRA and ASIC in an open, constructive and cooperative way
Personally approving every customer complaint outcome in their division
Holding a minimum shareholding in the bank for the duration of their appointment
Signing every WHS risk assessment
quiz.explanation: Section 21(1)(b) requires accountable persons to deal with the Regulator in an open, constructive and cooperative way. The other options are not FAR obligations.

quiz.question: Under the FAR Act, how much of an accountable person's variable remuneration must generally be deferred?
options: At least 10%
At least 40% for the relevant financial year
At least 25%
All of it, until retirement
quiz.explanation: Section 27(1) sets the required deferred amount at 40% of the accountable person's variable remuneration for the relevant financial year, deferred for at least the minimum deferral period.

quiz.question: What can the Regulator do if satisfied that an accountable person has failed to meet their accountability obligations and that it is justified by the seriousness of the failure?
options: Disqualify the person from being or acting as an accountable person
Fine the person's family members
Cancel the bank's banking licence automatically and appoint an administrator
Order the person to repay all past salary
quiz.explanation: Section 42 allows the Regulator to disqualify a person for a period it considers appropriate, having regard to the seriousness of the failure.

quiz.question: Which matter must a whistleblower policy under s 1317AI set out?
options: The names of past whistleblowers and the outcome of each of their disclosures to date
How the company will ensure fair treatment of employees mentioned in disclosures
The amount of any reward paid to whistleblowers under the bank's speak-up scheme
The salary of the whistleblower protection officer
quiz.explanation: Section 1317AI(5)(e) requires information on fair treatment of employees mentioned in or affected by disclosures. Naming whistleblowers would breach confidentiality.

quiz.question: What did ASIC's RG 270 say about whistleblower training?
options: Training is prohibited because it may identify whistleblowers
Entities should provide upfront and ongoing training, with specialist training for eligible recipients
Training is only needed for board directors
Training must be delivered by ASIC staff
quiz.explanation: RG 270 expects upfront and ongoing education and training on the policy and specialist training for eligible recipients and others handling disclosures.

quiz.question: APRA's 2018 prudential inquiry into CBA found which of the following?
options: That CBA had no board risk committee
That CBA's capital was below the legal minimum and it needed emergency funding
That CBA's whistleblower policy was missing and had never been reviewed by the board
Unclear accountabilities and remuneration with little sting for poor risk outcomes
quiz.explanation: The panel found unclear accountabilities, weak escalation and remuneration with little sting for senior managers, among other cultural issues. APRA then applied a AUD 1 billion capital add-on.

quiz.question: Which evidence best shows the board that the bank meets the WHS training duty in s 19(3)(f) for contact centre staff?
options: Role-based training linked to assessed risks, with completion, effectiveness checks and HSR feedback
A copy of the WHS policy approved by the board, with the date and minutes of approval and the policy owner's sign-off
A list of staff who opened the policy email
The number of WHS incidents reported to the regulator
quiz.explanation: Section 19(3)(f) looks at the training necessary to protect people. Evidence linking training to risks, and checking it works, shows that; policy approval or email opens do not.

regulators: State and territory WHS regulators and Comcare (Commonwealth), with Safe Work Australia as national policy body

bank.question: A labour hire worker placed in Tasman Ridge's mail room is injured using a faulty franking machine. The labour hire firm says it is responsible for her safety. Which is correct?
options: Only the labour hire firm owes her a duty, because it is her employer and pays her wages
The bank also owes her the primary duty, because she carries out work for the bank as a PCBU
The bank owes a duty only if she is on its payroll and her contract is with the bank directly
Neither owes a duty, since she is a temporary worker
bank.explanation: Section 7 includes labour hire employees assigned to the business as workers, and s 19 applies to workers engaged or directed by the PCBU. More than one PCBU can owe duties at once.

bank.question: Tasman Ridge introduces a new cash recycler in branches. Staff get a two-page leaflet but no demonstration, and two tellers jam their fingers clearing it. Which part of the primary duty is most directly in question?
options: Providing adequate welfare facilities
Providing the information, training, instruction or supervision necessary to protect people from the risk
Monitoring workers' health
Keeping notifiable incident records
bank.explanation: The issue is whether the instruction and training given were necessary and adequate for the new plant, which is s 19(3)(f). Safe plant under (b) is also relevant, but the gap described is in training.

bank.question: A contact centre manager says a full call-handling course for new starters is too expensive, so the bank only needs to email the policy. How should cost be treated under s 18?
options: Cost is the first factor, and any control above the team's budget can be dropped in favour of cheaper ones each year
Cost cannot be considered at all
Cost is weighed last and a control can be rejected on cost only if the cost is grossly disproportionate to the risk
Cost decides the matter if the budget has been approved by the board for that financial year's safety plan
bank.explanation: Section 18(e) brings cost in after assessing the risk and available controls, asking whether it is grossly disproportionate to the risk. It is not a first-order budget test.

bank.question: James, the COO, receives a safety dashboard but never asks whether the training reported as 'complete' actually took place. Which element of officer due diligence is weakest?
options: Verifying the provision and use of resources and processes
Acquiring knowledge of WHS matters
Understanding the general nature of the operations of the business and its hazards
Having processes for receiving incident information
bank.explanation: Section 27(5)(f) requires officers to verify the provision and use of the resources and processes in (c) to (e). Receiving a dashboard without checking is a verification gap.

bank.question: Which statement best describes how the Commonwealth WHS Act relates to workplaces across Australia?
options: It directly governs every workplace in Australia, replacing state and territory laws and regulators since 2011
It applies only to banks regulated by APRA
It follows the model law; states and territories have similar Acts, and Victoria has its own OHS Act
It replaced all state and territory safety laws in 2011
bank.explanation: The Commonwealth Act follows the model WHS law, and states and territories have mirror laws. Victoria has its own OHS Act, so learners must check which law applies.

bank.question: A customer slips on a wet floor near a branch ATM after cleaners mopped without signs. Does the bank's WHS duty extend to the customer?
options: No, WHS duties protect workers only, so customers must rely on negligence law
Yes, the PCBU must ensure others are not put at risk by work carried out in the business
Only if the customer is also a bank employee
Only if the cleaner was a bank employee rather than a contractor engaged by the branch manager
bank.explanation: Section 19(2) requires the PCBU to ensure, so far as reasonably practicable, that the health and safety of other persons is not put at risk from its work.

bank.question: A worker repeatedly ignores the notified procedure to lock the rear door before counting cash, saying it slows him down. Which is correct?
options: He breaches his own duty to cooperate with reasonable notified safety procedures, and the bank should address it
Only the bank has duties under the Act, so his conduct is a matter for performance management alone by the line manager
He has no duty because procedures are not law
Only the officer is liable for his conduct, under the officer's due diligence duty
bank.explanation: Section 28(d) requires workers to cooperate with reasonable notified policies and procedures. The bank still owes its own duties, including supervision.

bank.question: Tasman Ridge can either remove the need for after-dark cash transfers by using a security contractor, or train staff to do them more safely. Both are reasonably practicable. What does s 17 require?
options: Train staff, because training is always the preferred control under the Act and is cheaper in most branches
Choose whichever option is cheaper
Eliminate the risk by removing the task, since elimination comes first when reasonably practicable
Do both only if a regulator requires it following an inspection of the branches
bank.explanation: Section 17 requires elimination so far as reasonably practicable; minimisation is for risks that cannot reasonably be eliminated. Training may still support the remaining risks.

bank.question: Which example best shows the training duty being met for a genuinely new risk?
options: Staff are told the new model starts on Monday and to call security if anything goes wrong
Before a new branch model with solo staffing starts, staff practise lone-work and duress procedures and are supervised for the first weeks
The duress procedure is added to the intranet library with an email to all branch staff and managers
Branch managers are asked to sign that they have read the procedure
bank.explanation: Section 19(3)(f) focuses on what is necessary to protect people. Practical training and supervision before exposure fit the risk; publishing or signing documents may not.

bank.question: The bank plans to change the training procedure for collections staff from a classroom course to a short video. Must it consult affected workers?
options: No, training format is purely a management decision
Only if the union requests it
Yes, decisions about procedures for providing information and training are consultation matters
Only if a notifiable incident has occurred
bank.explanation: Section 49(e)(v) lists decisions about procedures for providing information and training to workers as a matter requiring consultation.

bank.question: A survey shows contact centre staff fear going home after shifts because of abusive callers. Which response is the strongest WHS control?
options: Redesign call handling with escalation, permission to end abusive calls and exposure limits
Add a wellbeing app to staff phones and promote the employee assistance program in team huddles every week
Remind staff the employee assistance program exists
Ask staff to toughen up during induction
bank.explanation: Work-design controls address the hazard at its source and should be reviewed with workers. Support services help but do not replace controls.

bank.question: A team leader asks why a worker's long-term stress injury from excessive workload was not notified to the regulator immediately. What is the best answer?
options: All psychological injuries must be notified within 48 hours
Notifiable incidents are deaths, serious injuries or illnesses as defined, and dangerous incidents; many psychological injuries are not, but they still must be recorded and managed internally
No injury involving stress can ever be notifiable
Only the worker can notify the regulator
bank.explanation: Sections 35-37 define notifiable incidents narrowly. Many psychosocial injuries fall outside them, but the primary duty still requires the risk to be managed.

bank.question: After a branch hold-up, a staff member is admitted to hospital as an in-patient. The manager wants to clean up and reopen within the hour. What should happen?
options: Reopen quickly to reassure customers, then notify the regulator within a week once the facts are known
Notify only the police, not the WHS regulator
Notify the regulator immediately and preserve the site, except for actions to help people or make it safe, until an inspector arrives or directs
Wait for written confirmation from the hospital before deciding
bank.explanation: In-patient treatment makes it a notifiable incident. Section 38 requires immediate notice, and s 39 requires the site to be preserved, subject to the listed exceptions.

bank.question: An HSR raises concerns about understaffing in a branch. Two weeks later, his manager removes him from the higher-paid relief manager roster, citing 'attitude'. What risk does the bank face?
options: None, because roster decisions are a management prerogative and are always lawful if a reason is given
Only a breach of the HSR's training entitlement and a possible breach of the duty to consult the work group
Only a notifiable incident report
A discriminatory conduct offence and civil claims if raising WHS concerns or his HSR role was the reason
bank.explanation: Sections 104-106 prohibit altering a worker's position to their detriment because they are an HSR or raised WHS issues. The offence requires the prohibited reason to be the dominant reason; civil proceedings are also available.

bank.question: Ben, as HSR, asks for approved training in May. In August the bank still has not released him, saying the roster is tight. Which is correct?
options: The bank may defer the course to the next financial year when rosters allow, as long as it pays the fees then
The bank may require Ben to take annual leave
The bank may choose a cheaper unapproved course instead
The bank must allow attendance as soon as practicable within three months of the request, with fees paid and time off with pay
bank.explanation: Section 72 requires release as soon as practicable within three months, payment of fees and reasonable costs, and paid time off. The HSR chooses the approved course.

bank.question: Which pair are both psychosocial hazards a bank should assess?
options: Glare on monitors and low job control in the contact centre
Heavy coin bags and unclear roles
Electrical faults and workplace conflict
Low job control and poor support from managers
bank.explanation: Low job control and poor support are both psychosocial hazards. Each other option pairs a psychosocial hazard with a physical one.

bank.question: What does consultation require the bank to do with workers' views?
options: Adopt every view a majority of workers holds, unless the board decides otherwise by resolution of directors
Record them but not consider them in the WHS committee minutes for future reference
Pass them to the regulator for decision
Take them into account when making the decision and advise workers of the outcome in a timely way
bank.explanation: Section 48 requires that workers' views are taken into account and that they are advised of the outcome in a timely manner. Consultation does not mean agreement.

bank.question: A regional bank with 40 staff and a major bank with 30,000 staff both ask what the positive duty requires. Which is correct?
options: Both must take reasonable and proportionate measures, but what is reasonable depends on size, nature, circumstances and resources
Only the major bank has the duty, because the Act exempts employers with fewer than 100 staff from it
Both must take exactly the same measures
Small employers are exempt until they receive a complaint
bank.explanation: Section 47C applies to all employers and PCBUs, and s 47C(6) makes size, nature, circumstances and resources relevant to what is reasonable and proportionate.

bank.question: A senior manager displays sexualised images in a shared office that several women staff must pass. No one is directly targeted. Which conduct is most clearly engaged?
options: Subjecting people to a workplace environment that is hostile on the ground of sex
Sex discrimination in recruitment
Victimisation
A personal work-related grievance
bank.explanation: Section 28M covers conduct that makes a workplace environment offensive, intimidating or humiliating on the ground of sex, even without targeting one person. Section 47C requires the bank to work to eliminate it.

bank.question: A relationship manager argues the bank cannot restrict a high-value client who harasses staff because he is not an employee. Which response is correct?
options: He is right; the Sex Discrimination Act positive duty only covers conduct by the bank's own employees and agents, not clients
The bank may act only if the client agrees to training
The bank must refer the matter to ASIC
The positive duty covers harassment of the bank's employees and workers by third parties, so the bank must take reasonable and proportionate measures
bank.explanation: Section 47C(4) covers sexual and sex-based harassment of the duty holder's employees and workers by any person, which includes clients.

bank.question: After Mia raised concerns informally, her team leader starts excluding her from meetings. Mia has not made a formal complaint. Is this within the positive duty?
options: No, victimisation is covered only after a formal written complaint to the Commission or a court
Yes, victimisation linked to allegations about covered conduct is within the duty even without a formal complaint
No, exclusion from meetings is not detriment
Only if Mia resigns as a result
bank.explanation: Section 47C covers victimisation, within the meaning of s 47A, relating to complaints, proceedings, assertions or allegations, which include informal allegations.

bank.question: The AHRC suspects a bank is not complying with the positive duty. What must it do after starting an inquiry?
options: Issue an immediate fine and publish the bank's name on its website
Refer the bank directly to APRA, which then decides whether to inquire and what findings to make about compliance
Publish the bank's name before contacting it
Give the bank written notice of the grounds for the inquiry and a reasonable opportunity to make submissions before any finding of non-compliance
bank.explanation: Section 35C requires written notice of the grounds as soon as practicable, and a reasonable opportunity to make oral or written submissions before a finding of non-compliance.

bank.question: Tasman Ridge receives a compliance notice and believes it is wrong. Within what time can it ask the President to reconsider?
options: Within 7 days
Within 90 days
Within 21 days after the notice is given
At any time before the court hearing on the compliance notice in the Federal Court
bank.explanation: Section 35G(2)(c) requires the request for reconsideration to be in writing, with reasons, within 21 days after the notice is given.

bank.question: Which plan is most likely to be a reasonable and proportionate response to known harassment risks at a large bank's conferences?
options: Ask attendees to sign a code of conduct on arrival and take no other action, since signing shows the bank set clear expectations for everyone
Cancel all events permanently without assessing the risk
Rely on attendees to report problems to police
Assess event risks, set controls on alcohol and timing, brief leaders, publicise reporting channels and follow up
bank.explanation: Preventive measures linked to identified risks, with leadership, reporting and follow-up, fit the purpose of s 47C. A signature alone does little, and cancelling without assessment is not risk-based.

bank.question: How do the positive duty and WHS duties interact for sexual harassment at a bank?
options: Sexual harassment is both covered by s 47C and a psychosocial hazard under WHS laws, and s 47C does not limit WHS duties
The positive duty replaced WHS duties for harassment matters, so only the Commission now deals with them
WHS laws apply only to physical harassment
The bank must choose which law to comply with
bank.explanation: Section 47C(7) preserves WHS duties. Harassment is a psychosocial risk under WHS laws and also within the positive duty, so both frameworks apply.

bank.question: A bank's external IT supplier's employee discovers that a bank system is overriding customer hardship flags, causing unlawful default fees. She tells the bank's chief risk officer. Does the disclosure qualify for protection?
options: No, only the bank's own employees can be whistleblowers, so she should tell her own employer instead
Yes, she is an employee of a supplier, the CRO is an eligible recipient, and she has reasonable grounds to suspect a contravention
No, disclosures must be made to ASIC first
Only if she discloses her name
bank.explanation: Section 1317AAA(d) covers employees of suppliers, s 1317AAC covers officers and senior managers as eligible recipients, and s 1317AA(5)(c) covers contraventions of credit law. Anonymity is allowed.

bank.question: A whistleblower's disclosure about loan file tampering also reveals that she personally altered two files. What does s 1317AB do?
options: It gives her full immunity for everything the disclosure reveals
It gives no protection because she was involved
It protects her from liability for making the disclosure, but not for her own misconduct revealed by it
It allows the bank to dismiss her for the disclosure
bank.explanation: Section 1317AB(1) prevents liability for making the disclosure, and its note confirms she may still be liable for her own conduct revealed by it (subject to the evidence rule in (1)(c)).

bank.question: An internal investigator, without naming the discloser, tells the team leader that 'the report came from someone in the evening shift who joined in March', and only one person fits. What is the problem?
options: None, because the name itself was not given and the investigator was acting in good faith
It is only a problem if the team leader repeats it
It is allowed because investigators may share anything
He disclosed information likely to lead to identification, which s 1317AAE prohibits unless an exception applies
bank.explanation: Section 1317AAE covers both identity and information likely to lead to identification. Investigation sharing must exclude identity and involve all reasonable steps to reduce the risk of identification.

bank.question: Which disclosure would be protected even though it is not made to ASIC, APRA or an eligible recipient?
options: A disclosure to a lawyer to get advice about how the whistleblower protections apply
A disclosure posted on social media
A disclosure to a friend at another bank
A disclosure to a journalist on day one
bank.explanation: Section 1317AA(3) protects disclosures to a legal practitioner for advice or representation about Part 9.4AAA. Public or media disclosures need the strict public interest or emergency conditions.

bank.question: A whistleblower reported a fire safety risk to APRA. She reasonably believes it poses a substantial and imminent danger to people's safety. What must she do before an emergency disclosure to a member of Parliament?
options: Wait at least 90 days
Get the bank's consent
Give APRA written notice identifying the earlier disclosure and stating she intends to make an emergency disclosure
Obtain a court order
bank.explanation: Section 1317AAD(2) requires a previous qualifying disclosure, reasonable grounds about substantial and imminent danger, and written notice to the body that received it. The 90-day wait applies to public interest disclosures, not emergency ones.

bank.question: A manager emails his team: 'Whoever went to ASIC should think about their future here.' No one is named and no action follows. Has he contravened s 1317AC?
options: Possibly yes, because threatening detriment, expressly or by implication, can be a contravention even without action
No, because no detriment actually occurred and the email named no one
No, because he did not know who reported
Only if someone proves they were afraid
bank.explanation: Section 1317AC(2) covers threats, which may be express or implied and conditional or unconditional, and s 1317AC(5) says it is not necessary to prove actual fear.

bank.question: A company officer was knowingly involved in the bank's victimisation of a whistleblower. Can a court order the officer to pay compensation?
options: Yes, the court can make orders against an officer knowingly concerned in the detrimental conduct
No, only the bank can be ordered to compensate
Only if the officer is a director
Only if ASIC brings criminal charges
bank.explanation: Section 1317AD(2) allows orders against an officer or employee who aided, induced or was knowingly concerned in the body corporate's detrimental conduct.

bank.question: Which matters can be disclosable matters for a bank whistleblower?
options: Suspected breaches of the Banking Act, the FAR Act or credit legislation, or conduct dangerous to the financial system
Only suspected criminal offences with prison terms over 10 years
Only breaches of the Corporations Act
Only matters affecting the whistleblower personally, such as pay, promotion or rosters
bank.explanation: Section 1317AA(5) lists contraventions of the Corporations Act, ASIC Act, Banking Act, FAR Act, NCCP Act and others, Commonwealth offences punishable by 12 months or more, and dangers to the public or financial system.

bank.question: In ASIC v TerraCom, which outcome did ASIC describe as a first?
options: Its first criminal conviction of a bank CEO
Its first action against an APRA-regulated insurer
Its first enforcement outcome for contraventions of the whistleblower provisions
Its first enforceable undertaking on harassment
bank.explanation: ASIC's release on the AUD 7.5 million penalty in 2025 described it as ASIC's first enforcement outcome for contraventions of whistleblower provisions.

bank.question: Tasman Ridge appoints a new chief people officer with senior executive responsibility for a significant part of the bank's operations. What must the bank consider under FAR?
options: Nothing, because FAR covers only the CEO and directors
Whether she is an accountable person who must be registered, with an accountability statement covering her responsibilities
Only whether she holds an AFS licence or an Australian credit licence in her own name
Whether she has completed WHS officer training within 30 days of starting and passed an APRA-approved assessment from Comcare
bank.explanation: Section 10 makes a person with actual or effective senior executive responsibility for a significant part of operations an accountable person; the bank must register accountable persons and give accountability statements.

bank.question: Which FAR obligation makes sure no part of the bank's operations is left without an accountable person?
options: The key personnel obligations
The deferred remuneration obligations
The whistleblower policy obligation
The notifiable incident obligation
bank.explanation: Section 23 requires the bank to ensure accountable persons' responsibilities cover all parts of the relevant group's operations.

bank.question: A bank argues that because it reduced an accountable person's bonus for a failure in the current year, it cannot reduce deferred amounts from earlier years. Which is correct?
options: Reductions can only apply to the year of the failure
Deferred amounts can never be reduced
Only the regulator can reduce variable remuneration
A reduction need not relate to the period of the failure and may be a reduction to zero
bank.explanation: Section 25(2) provides that a reduction need not relate to the period in which the failure occurred and may reduce variable remuneration to zero.

bank.question: Tasman Ridge's whistleblower policy is approved but sits on a page staff cannot find, and eligible recipients have never been trained. What is the most accurate assessment?
options: It is fully compliant and nothing more is needed
It is unlawful because ASIC must approve the policy before it takes effect, and the bank has not sought approval
It is irrelevant because banks are exempt from s 1317AI
It may meet the bare legal requirement, but falls short of ASIC's guidance on training and accessibility and risks failures in handling disclosures
bank.explanation: Section 1317AI requires a policy covering set matters and made available to officers and employees. RG 270 expects ongoing training and specialist training for eligible recipients; untrained recipients risk breaching confidentiality.

bank.question: APRA's 2018 CBA inquiry linked weak non-financial risk management to which accountability issue later addressed by FAR-style rules?
options: A shortage of branch staff
A lack of clear ownership of key risks at executive level and pay with little consequence for poor risk outcomes
Unclear WHS notification forms and branch safety reporting templates
Excessive use of whistleblower hotlines that overwhelmed the bank's compliance and legal teams for years in a row
bank.explanation: The panel found unclear accountabilities and remuneration with little sting for senior managers. FAR's accountability maps and deferred remuneration address those themes.

bank.question: The board risk committee asks for whistleblower program reporting. Which approach is appropriate?
options: A list of disclosers and their business units, so directors can follow up personally with each one where needed
Aggregated trends, themes, timeliness and outcomes, with no information likely to identify disclosers
Copies of every disclosure in full, including attachments and the names of witnesses
Only the number of disclosures, with no themes or outcomes
bank.explanation: Boards need meaningful oversight information, but s 1317AAE prohibits disclosing identity or information likely to identify whistleblowers. Aggregated reporting balances both.

bank.question: An accountable person learns that a branch network has ignored HSR concerns about staff safety for a year and does nothing. Which FAR obligation is most at risk?
options: The obligation to defer 40% of every employee's pay
Taking reasonable steps to prevent matters that would adversely affect the bank's prudential standing or reputation
The obligation to file the bank's annual tax return
The obligation to hold a credit licence
bank.explanation: Section 21(1)(c) requires accountable persons to take reasonable steps in their responsibilities to prevent matters likely to damage prudential standing or reputation; ignoring known people-safety failures engages it.

bank.question: Which combination best evidences a bank's people-safety program to a regulator?
options: Approved policies and an annual staff email
Training completion percentages only
Risk assessments, role-based training records with effectiveness checks, consultation records, harassment prevention measures, whistleblower metrics and named accountabilities
A record of disciplinary outcomes, the names of staff disciplined and the policies breached, collected over three years
bank.explanation: Regulators look for evidence that risks are assessed, controls and training work, workers are consulted and accountability is clear. Policies or single metrics alone do not show that.
